title: “Toad” Packs Four Cylinders of Ford Banger Fury

body_markdown:
We spotted this 1929 Ford Model A at Bonneville Speed Week 2025, just a few months after it was completed. Blaine West and his father made the trip to the salt flats from their home in Carlton, Oregon, to catch some land speed racing in the Model A that the recent high school grad had built himself. We tagged along to get some photos near the salt, and as you’ll see, the bare-bones coupe seems right at home at Bonneville.


[Brandan Gillogly](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/brandan-gillogly/)


West had spent the past couple of years scavenging parts for the car, which he had noticed for sale on Instagram, posted by an account his dad followed. “I got the car up in Bow, Washington, which is about 25 minutes from the border of Canada,” West said. He and his dad made the seven-hour drive to see it in person. It had been converted into a pickup at some point, so the quarter panels were rather hacked up. West had planned to build a Model A, and he’d already picked up an original pair of quarters that were in solid shape, so that wouldn’t be an issue. We’re not sure whether West was able to hide his enthusiasm, because he told us that he immediately fell for the car and “thought it was meant to be.” The seller seemed to feel that the Model A body would have a good home and struck a deal. “I spent my very first paycheck for my very first job on it,” said West. He was just 14 at the time.


With a limited budget and plenty of other obligations, West didn’t make much progress on the build until two years later. That’s when he spotted a good deal on a chassis on Facebook Marketplace. Then the project really got kickstarted. Once he got the chassis home, West refreshed the original engine and got it running. He also serviced the transmission and got it in working order. “I built a whole front suspension,” he said. It rides on a 1934 Ford drop axle up front, but it wasn’t quite low enough for his liking. “I reverse-eyed the main front spring by myself,” West explained, “to lower it another two inches.” He and his father fabricated the rear subframe, which had completely rusted out of the car.


The iron Winfield head increased compression from 4.22:1 to 6:1. Doing some quick, speculative math, bumping the compression that significantly could increase power by more than 20% on its own, even ignoring any airflow gains from the new combustion chamber.


[Brandan Gillogly](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/brandan-gillogly/)


The engine sounded great and didn’t have any trouble getting the featherweight coupe up to speed. It hasn’t been on a dyno, and West is definitely not under the impression that it’s a powerhouse, but he appreciates the added output he’s been able to squeeze from the Ford banger. “I built my own intake manifold for it, for a Holley 94,” West said, referencing the vintage two-barrel. “It’s got a Winfield high-compression head,” he added. And what, exactly, does “high compression” mean in the world of Ford flathead four-cylinders? “Oh, high compression’s about six to one,” he said with a laugh. West reminded us that Model As made the big switch to electric start, although there was still a provision to crank it by hand like its Model T predecessor. Anyone having to turn a 3.3-liter engine by hand would be thankful for a low compression ratio.

Blaine West kept the car’s original motor, original transmission, and original rear end. The 1933–34 Ford 17-inch wheels use 5.50-inch tires in the front and 7.50-inch tires in the rear.[Brandan Gillogly](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/brandan-gillogly/)


We asked West about the car’s nickname painted on the quarter panel. “It was really inspired by a hot rod that was built in the ’50s. It was a drag car called the ‘Loaded Toad.’ I always loved the name and didn’t really want to copy it. It’s not really my thing, copying people’s names. But after putting together a car, I mean, it was green, it was short, it was snotty-looking, it croaked.” It’s hard to argue; the name fits. West used some of his mom’s paint and added the moniker in time to race it at a dirt track event that high school teacher and[Taco Coupe owner Charlie Haskell](https://www.hagerty.com/media/car-profiles/taco-coupe-high-schoolers-unfolded-a-ford-into-this-hot-rod-racer/) put on.


In addition to the influence from his father, West has been encouraged to build his car by his fellow employees at the shop where he’s an apprentice diesel mechanic. “My boss is into hot rods, my coworkers are into hot rods, so we all go to the same events,” West said. “I’ve been very fortunate to be connected to a tight group of people that are all into the same stuff.”


In addition to swapping on the set of salvaged quarter panels, West chopped five inches out of the doors and windshield pillar. Although he’s an adept mechanic, he’s picking up bodywork from his father. “I did the quarters and the rear subframe with my dad; he taught me a lot of sheet metal work,” he explained.


[Brandan Gillogly](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/brandan-gillogly/)


The Toad is currently dressed like a sport coupe sans roof; West has plans to build a standard coupe roof to return it to its roots. “I think I’m gonna try to match it to the car first and paint it later down the road,” he explained. The goal is to keep the car looking like a traditional racing hot rod. “I want it to look like a kid in 1941 or 1940 had a Model A sport coupe … and it was his daily driver that he could go out and race on the weekends.” That means there’s no small-block V-8 swap planned, but it seems Blaine West is still on the hunt for more power. Perhaps there are some rare speed parts on the horizon. “My holy grail part would probably be a Riley two-port overhead-valve conversion for the banger. My dream is to have a really, really nasty little four-cylinder in it. I’ve thought about going to a V-8,” he added, noting that a Ford flathead would still fit his vintage racer formula, “but with this car, it just keeps telling me to keep the banger in it.”

## Model A Trivia:


In 1929, in addition to the standard roadster, the Ford Model A was also available in several sporty, two-door flavors: standard coupe, special coupe, sport coupe, and cabriolet. The roadster uses thin windshield pillars and has no side windows and no window framing around the door. The standard coupe had a steel top, with the exception of the fabric center section. It had roll-down door glass with a full metal frame, and it used a steel visor over the windshield. Special coupes, often called “Leatherback Coupes” are similar to standard coupes but had the same roof fabric applied to the C-pillar and around the rear window. Cabriolets, with their complex folding top, also have door glass, but it’s only framed at the front. They use a thicker A-pillar than a roadster and have three door hinges, just like a coupe, but have no visor over the windshield. The sport coupe has a fixed top that mimics the cabriolet. It uses fully framed doors and sports a steel windshield visor like other Model A coupes.
